screens.title: What are Events and Why Use Them?
screens.narratorSegment: An event in Solidity is a logging mechanism that writes data to the transaction's log rather than to contract storage. This makes events uniquely suited for off‑chain communication. When you emit an event, the EVM records it in the transaction receipt; off‑chain systems, such as front ends or backend listeners, can subscribe to those logs, filter them by indexed fields, and respond to contract activity without continuously querying the contract state. A concrete example: emitting a Transfer event when tokens move lets a wallet update balances in real time by listening for that transfer, rather than polling every account balance. A common misconception is that events are a replacement for persistent state; they are not. Event logs are cheaper and ideal for broadcasting facts, but not reliable for on‑chain logic because contracts cannot read past logs. Another useful point: events are gas‑efficient because they avoid storage writes and store data in logs. The teaching takeaway is simple: use events for observability and off‑chain signals, but rely on contract state for on‑chain decisions. Ask yourself: which data should be in state and which should be emitted as an event for off‑chain tools to consume?

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › What are Events?
Definition

Events are transaction logs

Events write structured data to transaction logs. Off‑chain systems read these logs to react to contract activity.

Why use events?
  • Gas‑cheaper than persistent storage.
  • Designed for off‑chain filtering and indexing.
  • Emit for all meaningful state transitions.
Concrete example

Emit Transfer(address indexed from, address indexed to, uint value) when tokens move. Wallets subscribe to that event to update UI quickly.

Key Takeaway

Use events to broadcast actions for off‑chain systems; don't rely on logs for contract state.

Analogy & Flow
Contract emits
Logs a structured message when a state change occurs.
Transaction logs
Stored in receipt and retrievable by tools.
Off‑chain listener
Filters by indexed fields and updates UI or backend processes.
// Example declaration
event Transfer(address indexed from, address indexed to, uint value);

// Emit on transfer
// emit Transfer(msg.sender, recipient, amount);

screens.title: Declare and Emit Events
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through declaring and emitting events with a practical deposit and withdrawal example. First, declare an event at contract scope using the event keyword and list parameter types. You can mark up to three parameters as indexed to allow off‑chain tools to filter logs by those values. For example, declare event Deposit(address indexed user, uint amount, uint newBalance);. The user parameter is indexed so you can query all deposits by a specific address. Emitting an event uses the emit keyword: emit Deposit(msg. sender, msg. value, address(this). balance);. In the deposit function you should validate inputs—if msg. value is zero you may revert—then update balances and emit the Deposit event. For withdrawals, after necessary checks, transfer the funds and emit a Withdrawal event with the updated balance. A common mistake is indexing every argument; remember the three‑indexed limit and that non‑indexed fields are still logged but cannot be filtered directly. Another confusion is thinking events replace state; they don't. Always update contract state for on‑chain logic, and use events alongside state changes for visibility. Practice emitting for every meaningful mutation so your DApp can reconstruct activity from logs.

keyIdea.title: Emit routinely

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › Declare & Emit
Syntax

event & emit

Declare events at contract scope and emit them inside functions with the emit keyword.

// Event declaration
event Deposit(address indexed user, uint amount, uint newBalance);

function deposit() public payable {
  if (msg.value == 0) revert();
  balances[msg.sender] += msg.value;
  emit Deposit(msg.sender, msg.value, balances[msg.sender]);
}
Common mistake

Indexing all fields or relying on events for on‑chain decisions. Events are for off‑chain listeners and auditing; keep authoritative state in contract storage.

Practical Notes
Index up to three parameters for efficient queries. Use address fields as indexed when you expect listeners to filter by account.
Non‑indexed parameters are included in logs but must be retrieved after filtering by indexed fields.
Emit for transparency: deposits, withdrawals, ownership changes, mints, burns, and transfers.
Try this

Add Deposit and Withdrawal events to an existing contract and inspect the transaction log in Remix after calling deposit and withdraw.

screens.title: How Off‑Chain Listeners Use Events
screens.narratorSegment: Off‑chain listeners—wallets, backends, or explorers—rely on events to efficiently observe contract activity. The typical flow is: a transaction executes and emits events; the EVM stores those events in transaction logs; indexers or nodes surface the logs and provide APIs to query them; listeners subscribe to filters to receive matching events. The indexed keyword on up to three event parameters is the mechanism that enables query filters. For example, marking from and to as indexed in a Transfer event allows a UI to request all transfers involving a specific address. Non‑indexed parameters are still part of the log payload but cannot be used directly in a filter query; they are retrieved after the filter identifies candidate logs. A common misunderstanding is expecting logs to be accessible in the same way as contract state inside solidity: contracts cannot read past logs for logic. Another important practice is designing events with the right granularity: include the minimum necessary data to reconstruct off‑chain state while avoiding redundancy. In the live coding you'll see how a listener uses indexed fields to fetch matching logs and then reads non‑indexed payloads to display amounts or balances.

keyIdea.text: Listeners filter by indexed parameters, retrieve matching logs, and then parse non‑indexed payloads to reconstruct activity.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › Off‑Chain Listeners
Process Flow

From emit to UI

A clear sequence connects on‑chain emits to off‑chain updates.

1. Transaction
Function runs and emits events when state changes succeed.
2. Logs stored
Event data is written to transaction logs in the receipt.
3. Indexing
Nodes or indexers expose APIs to query logs by indexed fields.
4. Listener
A UI or backend subscribes to filters and processes the returned log payloads.
Indexing tip: index the fields you will filter by, such as addresses or identifiers.
Recovery tip: store authoritative state on‑chain; use logs to reconstruct views, not to enforce contract logic.
Example scenario

A DApp subscribes to Transfer events indexed by recipient address to show incoming transactions instantly without polling every account balance.

screens.title: Indexed vs Non‑Indexed Event Parameters
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding indexed versus non‑indexed parameters is essential for designing events that are both useful and efficient. Indexed parameters are stored in the log's topics and can be searched or filtered by off‑chain tools. You can index up to three parameters. For example, in Transfer(address indexed from, address indexed to, uint value), from and to become topics that indexers can search for quickly; value remains part of the data payload and must be read after a match is found. Non‑indexed parameters are included in the log data and are retrievable but not filterable at query time. The practical tradeoff is: index the fields you will frequently filter on, such as user addresses or token ids, and leave large or seldom‑filtered values non‑indexed to save topic slots. A misconception is that indexing always increases gas dramatically; while topics cost gas, using them correctly enables powerful queries that save developer time and off‑chain computation. The takeaway: choose indexed fields deliberately and remember the three‑indexed limit when designing event signatures. Indexed vs Non‑Indexed Event Parameters means index fields you will search for; leave other data in payload to preserve topic slots and reduce unnecessary indexing costs.. In practical terms, when to index and what it buys you. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › Indexed vs Non‑Indexed
Indexed

Searchable topics

Indexed parameters appear in topics and support efficient filtering by tools and explorers.

  • Up to three indexed parameters.
  • Ideal for addresses and IDs you will query often.
  • Used by wallets and backends to fetch relevant logs quickly.
Non‑Indexed

Payload data

Non‑indexed parameters live in the log data. They are retrievable after a filter identifies matching logs but cannot be used as filter criteria.

  • Good for amounts, balances, or metadata not used in queries.
  • Less flexible for listener filtering, but preserves topic slots.
Example: index from and to in Transfer to find transfers involving an address.
Caution: do not expect contracts to read logs; logs are for off‑chain only.
Design tip: prefer a small, stable event schema so DApps can depend on consistent topics.

screens.title: Transaction Logs and Gas Efficiency
screens.narratorSegment: Transaction logs are stored separately from contract storage and are optimized for event data. Writing to storage changes the contract state and is relatively expensive; logs provide a cheaper alternative for recording occurrences you only need off‑chain. When you emit an event the data lands in the transaction receipt and is not part of contract storage. This distinction is important for gas budgeting: use events to record audit trails, notifications, or history that will be consumed off‑chain, while keeping the minimum necessary state variables on‑chain for governance or future on‑chain checks. An important misconception to avoid is assuming logs are immutable and accessible for on‑chain verification—contracts cannot read logs contents to make logic decisions. Another practical point: emitting many events in a single transaction will still cost gas, so design event frequency and payload size thoughtfully. For example, for high‑volume systems you might emit aggregated events or less detailed logs to balance observability with cost. The key insight: events are a tool for visibility and efficiency, not a substitute for authoritative state. Transaction Logs and Gas Efficiency means logs are gas‑efficient for off‑chain visibility; storage is authoritative for on‑chain logic.. In practical terms, why logs are cheaper and when to prefer them. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › Transaction Logs
Gas Efficiency

Logs are cheaper than storage

Because logs don't change contract storage, emitting events generally consumes less gas than writing state. Use them for off‑chain signals.

Audit trail: emit events for operations you want recorded for explorers or backends.
Design: avoid emitting excessively large payloads; include only necessary fields to reconstruct the event off‑chain.
Scaling: for high frequency operations, consider aggregated events or off‑chain batching where appropriate.
Misconception

Contracts cannot rely on logs as source of truth. Logs are for off‑chain consumption only and cannot be read during contract execution.

Why it matters

Choosing between logs and storage influences gas costs, UX, and what your contract can verify on‑chain.

screens.title: Custom Errors: Structured and Gas‑Efficient
screens.narratorSegment: Custom errors, added in Solidity 0.8.4, let you declare typed exceptions with parameters and then revert with them. They are gas‑efficient because the error's textual string is not stored on‑chain; instead the error selector and arguments are encoded. Declare custom errors with the error keyword, for example: error InsufficientBalance(uint currentBalance, uint requestedAmount);. When a check fails, use revert InsufficientBalance(balances[msg. sender], _amount);. Off‑chain tooling decodes the error selector and arguments so you can present precise diagnostics to users. A concrete usage: in a transfer function check if balances[msg. sender] < _amount and revert with InsufficientBalance. A common confidence error is to rely only on string messages in require; strings are convenient but cost more gas and are harder for programs to parse. Use custom errors for structured failure modes that your DApp will handle programmatically. Remember that custom errors are declared at contract level or globally and that revert will roll back state changes as usual. The practical outcome: clearer errors, lower gas, and better automation for error handling in UIs. In practical terms, declare, revert, and read structured error data. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › Custom Errors
Declare
// Custom error declarations
error InsufficientBalance(uint currentBalance, uint requestedAmount);
error NotOwner(address caller);
Declare errors at contract scope and reuse them across functions that need the same structured revert. They encode a selector and arguments rather than a literal string, yielding gas savings.
Use
function transfer(address _to, uint _amount) public {
  if (balances[msg.sender] < _amount) {
    revert InsufficientBalance(balances[msg.sender], _amount);
  }
  // transfer logic...
}
Off‑chain tools decode the revert data so your UI can show a precise error such as insufficient funds and the amounts involved.
Pitfall

Do not mix long descriptive strings and custom errors without reason. Prefer structured custom errors when UIs will parse the failure programmatically; keep simple require messages for quick debugging during development if needed.

screens.title: Using require, revert, and assert Correctly
screens.narratorSegment: Solidity provides three primary ways to enforce conditions: require, revert, and assert. Use require for input validation and expected state checks; it reverts and refunds remaining gas to the caller and is ideal for simple guard clauses at the start of functions. Revert is useful when you need to stop execution within a complex condition or when using custom errors: perform an if check and revert with a custom error to provide structured data. content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › Integrated Example
Example Contract
// Events
event FundsDeposited(address indexed user, uint amount, uint newBalance);
event FundsWithdrawn(address indexed user, uint amount, uint newBalance);

// Custom errors
error InsufficientFunds(address sender, uint requestedAmount, uint currentBalance);
error NotOwner(address caller);
error ZeroAmount();

function deposit() public payable {
  if (msg.value == 0) revert ZeroAmount();
  balances[msg.sender] += msg.value;
  emit FundsDeposited(msg.sender, msg.value, balances[msg.sender]);
}

function withdraw(uint _amount) public {
  if (msg.sender != owner) revert NotOwner(msg.sender);
  if (_amount == 0) revert ZeroAmount();
  if (balances[msg.sender] < _amount) revert InsufficientFunds(msg.sender, _amount, balances[msg.sender]);
  balances[msg.sender] -= _amount;
  payable(msg.sender).transfer(_amount);
  emit FundsWithdrawn(msg.sender, _amount, balances[msg.sender]);
}
What to observe

When deposit succeeds, listeners see FundsDeposited. When withdraw reverts, the UI receives a decoded InsufficientFunds error with amounts.

Why this pattern

Structured errors + events create clear contracts that are easy to debug and integrate with UIs.

screens.title: Practical Rules and Common Mistakes
screens.narratorSegment: To finish the lessons, let's collect practical rules and common pitfalls so your contracts are robust in production. First, fail early: put validation checks at the start of functions with require or revert to avoid wasting gas on operations that will fail. Second, prefer custom errors for cases where you need structured data or the message would be long; they are gas‑efficient and machine‑readable. Third, use assert only for invariants you believe cannot be violated; an assert failure means a contract bug. Fourth, emit events for every meaningful state change—deposits, withdrawals, transfers, mints, and ownership changes—so UIs and auditors can reconstruct activity. Common mistakes include indexing too many fields, expecting contracts to read logs, and using assert for input validation. Another pitfall is ambiguous require messages—be explicit when debugging, but refactor to custom errors before production to reduce gas. The final takeaway: observability and predictable error semantics are not optional; they make your DApp maintainable, debuggable, and trustworthy for users and integrators. In this lesson we will explore two tightly paired features of Solidity that make your contracts observable and resilient. First, events provide a lightweight, gas-efficient mechanism for contracts to log meaningful actions so off‑chain systems can react. You will learn how to declare events, use indexed parameters for fast filtering, and why logs are cheaper than storing state. Second, we'll introduce modern error handling using custom errors available since Solidity 0.8.4. Custom errors let you revert with structured data while saving gas compared with long error strings. Throughout the chapter we'll practice emitting events for common operations like deposits, withdrawals, transfers, and show how to declare and trigger custom errors such as InsufficientBalance or Unauthorized. You'll also learn practical rules: use require for input validation, revert with custom errors for complex logic, and assert only for internal invariants. By the end you'll understand why visibility into contract activity and precise, gas-aware error messages are essential for building production DApps and for troubleshooting on testnets and mainnet. Consider how your front end would subscribe to logs versus repeatedly polling the contract state as we go through examples.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to recognize when to use events in your contracts and how to design them so off‑chain systems can filter and react efficiently. Specifically, you'll declare and emit events with proper indexed parameters to support fast queries from UIs and backends. You will also explain how event logs differ from regular contract storage and why logs are a more gas‑efficient way to broadcast information. Finally, you'll begin to use Solidity's modern error handling: declaring custom errors and replacing long string messages with structured reverts. Throughout we'll emphasize practical practices: emitting events on meaningful state changes, limiting indexed fields to at most three for searchability, using require for simple checks, revert with custom errors for complex conditions, and reserving assert for internal invariants. These skills improve observability, save gas, and make your contracts easier to debug in production. A short exercise at the end asks you to add Transfer and Mint events to a simple token and refactor transfer logic to revert with a custom InsufficientBalance error.

This second objectives slide focuses on practical application and measurement. You'll practice declaring events like Transfer and Mint with indexed address fields and emitting them in transfer and mint functions so a UI can show live updates. You will also implement deposit and withdraw functions that emit Deposit and Withdrawal events including the new balance. For error handling exercises, you'll declare custom errors like InsufficientBalance and NotOwner, then use revert with those errors in transfer, withdraw, and owner‑only functions. We'll also run through sample transactions so you can inspect emitted logs in Remix or a block explorer and observe the encoded custom error returned on revert. These practical activities ground the concepts: seeing a log emitted makes it concrete why logs are cheaper than state writes, and triggering a custom error demonstrates clearer diagnostics and lower gas relative to long string messages. The live coding will include step‑by‑step refactors and tests to validate event emissions and custom error triggers so you can verify behavior during development.

An event in Solidity is a logging mechanism that writes data to the transaction's log rather than to contract storage. This makes events uniquely suited for off‑chain communication. When you emit an event, the EVM records it in the transaction receipt; off‑chain systems, such as front ends or backend listeners, can subscribe to those logs, filter them by indexed fields, and respond to contract activity without continuously querying the contract state. A concrete example: emitting a Transfer event when tokens move lets a wallet update balances in real time by listening for that transfer, rather than polling every account balance. A common misconception is that events are a replacement for persistent state; they are not. Event logs are cheaper and ideal for broadcasting facts, but not reliable for on‑chain logic because contracts cannot read past logs. Another useful point: events are gas‑efficient because they avoid storage writes and store data in logs. The teaching takeaway is simple: use events for observability and off‑chain signals, but rely on contract state for on‑chain decisions. Ask yourself: which data should be in state and which should be emitted as an event for off‑chain tools to consume?

Let's walk through declaring and emitting events with a practical deposit and withdrawal example. First, declare an event at contract scope using the event keyword and list parameter types. You can mark up to three parameters as indexed to allow off‑chain tools to filter logs by those values. For example, declare event Deposit(address indexed user, uint amount, uint newBalance);. Another confusion is thinking events replace state; they don't. Always update contract state for on‑chain logic, and use events alongside state changes for visibility. Practice emitting for every meaningful mutation so your DApp can reconstruct activity from logs.

Off‑chain listeners—wallets, backends, or explorers—rely on events to efficiently observe contract activity. The typical flow is: a transaction executes and emits events; the EVM stores those events in transaction logs; indexers or nodes surface the logs and provide APIs to query them; listeners subscribe to filters to receive matching events. The indexed keyword on up to three event parameters is the mechanism that enables query filters. For example, marking from and to as indexed in a Transfer event allows a UI to request all transfers involving a specific address. Non‑indexed parameters are still part of the log payload but cannot be used directly in a filter query; they are retrieved after the filter identifies candidate logs. A common misunderstanding is expecting logs to be accessible in the same way as contract state inside solidity: contracts cannot read past logs for logic. Another important practice is designing events with the right granularity: include the minimum necessary data to reconstruct off‑chain state while avoiding redundancy. In the live coding you'll see how a listener uses indexed fields to fetch matching logs and then reads non‑indexed payloads to display amounts or balances.

Understanding indexed versus non‑indexed parameters is essential for designing events that are both useful and efficient. Indexed parameters are stored in the log's topics and can be searched or filtered by off‑chain tools. You can index up to three parameters. For example, in Transfer(address indexed from, address indexed to, uint value), from and to become topics that indexers can search for quickly; value remains part of the data payload and must be read after a match is found. To finish the lessons, let's collect practical rules and common pitfalls so your contracts are robust in production. First, fail early: put validation checks at the start of functions with require or revert to avoid wasting gas on operations that will fail. Second, prefer custom errors for cases where you need structured data or the message would be long; they are gas‑efficient and machine‑readable. Third, use assert only for invariants you believe cannot be violated; an assert failure means a contract bug. Fourth, emit events for every meaningful state change—deposits, withdrawals, transfers, mints, and ownership changes—so UIs and auditors can reconstruct activity.
